accepted.question_text: Let C be an elliptic curve over Q, let L(C,s) be its L-series, and let rank(C(Q)) denote the rank of the finitely generated abelian group of rational points on C. Is the order of vanishing of L(C,s) at s=1 equal to rank(C(Q))? Equivalently, does the Taylor expansion of L(C,s) at s=1 have the form L(C,s)=c(s-1)^r + higher order terms with c != 0 and r = rank(C(Q)), so that L(C,1)=0 exactly when C(Q) is infinite?

evidence.quote: Conjecture (Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer). The Taylor expansion of L(C, s) at s = 1 has the form L(C, s) = c(s − 1)^r + higher order terms with c 6= 0 and r = rank(C(Q)). In particular this conjecture asserts that L(C, 1) = 0 ⇔ C(Q) is infinite.

accepted.question_text: For an elliptic curve C over Q, is the Tate-Shafarevich group X_C finite? The refined Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture involves |X_C|, but the source states that this group is not known in general to be finite, although it is conjectured to be so.

evidence.quote: Here |XC | is the order of the Tate–Shafarevich group of the elliptic curve C, a group which is not known in general to be finite although it is conjectured to be so.

accepted.question_text: Let V be an algebraic variety over Q, and remove from V the closures of all subvarieties that are images of P1 or of abelian varieties, obtaining an open subvariety W. Must W(Q), the set of rational points of W, be finite?

evidence.quote: In higher dimensions, if V is an algebraic variety, it is conjectured (see [14]) that if we remove from V (the closure of) all subvarieties that are images of P1 or of abelian varieties, then the remaining open variety W should have the property that W (Q) is finite.

accepted.question_text: If X is a projective nonsingular algebraic variety over C, is every Hodge class on X a rational linear combination of classes cl(Z) of algebraic cycles Z on X?

evidence.quote: Hodge Conjecture. On a projective non-singular algebraic variety over C, any Hodge class is a rational linear combination of classes cl(Z) of algebraic cycles.

accepted.question_text: Let X be a projective nonsingular variety and let J_p(X) be the extension involving the intermediate Jacobian that receives codimension-p algebraic cycles. If A_p(X) denotes the subgroup of J_p(X) generated by algebraic cycles, which subgroup of J_p(X) is A_p(X)?

evidence.quote: No conjecture is available to predict what subgroup of Jp (X) the group Ap (X) is.

accepted.question_text: Given an algebraic family of projective nonsingular algebraic varieties (X_s) over a parameter space S defined over the algebraic closure of Q in C, is there an algorithm that decides whether a given integral cohomology class of a typical fiber X_0 becomes of Hodge type (p,p) somewhere on S?

evidence.quote: No algorithm is known to decide whether a given integral cohomology class of a typical fiber X0 is somewhere on S of type (p, p).

accepted.question_text: Let A be an abelian variety over the algebraic closure F of a finite field F_q. Lift A in two different ways to characteristic 0, obtaining complex abelian varieties A1 and A2 defined over Q̄, and choose complementary-dimensional Hodge classes z1 and z2 on A1 and A2. After interpreting z1 and z2 as l-adic cohomology classes and reducing them over F, is the resulting intersection number κ always a rational number?

evidence.quote: Let A be an abelian variety over the algebraic closure F of a finite field Fq . Lift A in two different ways to characteristic 0, to complex abelian varieties A1 and A2 defined over Q̄. Pick Hodge classes z1 and z2 on A1 and A2 , of complementary dimension. Interpreting z1 and z2 as `-adic cohomology classes, one can define the intersection number κ of the reduction of z1 and z2 over F. Is κ a rational number?

accepted.question_text: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with viscosity ν > 0, must one of the standard global regularity statements hold: either smooth physically reasonable solutions always exist globally on R^3 or on the periodic domain R^3/Z^3 for smooth divergence-free initial data, or else there exist smooth data for which no such global smooth solution exists on one of those domains?

evidence.quote: A fundamental problem in analysis is to decide whether such smooth, physically reasonable solutions exist for the Navier–Stokes equations. To give reasonable leeway to solvers while retaining the heart of the problem, we ask for a proof of one of the following four statements.
(A) Existence and smoothness of Navier–Stokes solutions on R3 .
(B) Existence and smoothness of Navier–Stokes solutions in R3 /Z3 .
(C) Breakdown of Navier–Stokes solutions on R3 .
(D) Breakdown of Navier–Stokes Solutions on R3 /Z3 .

accepted.question_text: If a compact three-dimensional manifold M^3 has the property that every simple closed curve in M^3 can be continuously deformed to a point within M^3, must M^3 be homeomorphic to the 3-sphere S^3?

evidence.quote: Question. If a compact three-dimensional manifold M 3 has the property that every simple closed curve within the manifold can be deformed continuously to a point, does it follow that M 3 is homeomorphic to the sphere S 3 ?

accepted.question_text: Is every decision problem whose proposed solutions can be checked in polynomial time also solvable in polynomial time; equivalently, does P = NP?

evidence.quote: Problem Statement. Does P = NP?

accepted.question_text: Do all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) have real part equal to 1/2?

evidence.quote: Riemann Hypothesis. The nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) have real part equal to 1/2.

accepted.question_text: Is there, for the classical global setting of the Riemann zeta function and related L-functions, a theory that plays the same role that cohomology plays for zeta functions of varieties over a field of positive characteristic?

evidence.quote: Is there a theory in the global case, playing the same role as cohomology does for Zeta functions of varieties over a field of positive characteristic?

accepted.question_text: In the classical setting of the Riemann zeta function, is there an analogue of the Frobenius automorphism that would play the corresponding role it plays for varieties over finite fields?

evidence.quote: Is there an analogue of a Frobenius automorphism in the classical case?

accepted.question_text: Is there a general index theorem that could be used to prove the classical Riemann hypothesis?

evidence.quote: Is there a general index theorem by which one can prove the classical Riemann hypothesis?

accepted.question_text: For any compact simple gauge group G, does there exist a non-trivial quantum Yang-Mills theory on R^4 with a positive mass gap Δ > 0, with existence understood as establishing axiomatic properties at least as strong as those cited in the source?

evidence.quote: Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap. Prove that for any compact simple gauge group G, a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills theory exists on R4 and has a mass gap ∆ > 0. Existence includes establishing axiomatic properties at least as strong as those cited in [45, 35].

needs_review.question_text_raw: The Hodge conjecture is not known even in the following nice examples. Example 1. ... The Kunneth components cl(∆)a,b of cl(∆) are Hodge classes. Example 2. ... The class z is Hodge.

evidence.quote: The Hodge conjecture is not known even in the following nice examples.
Example 1. For X of complex dimension N , the diagonal ∆ of X × X is an algebraic cycle of codimension N . ... The Künneth components cl(∆)a,b ... are Hodge classes.
Example 2. ... The class z is Hodge.

needs_review.question_text_raw: There are many natural extensions of the Millennium problem. Among other things, one would like to prove the existence of an isolated one-particle state ..., to prove confinement, to prove existence of other four-dimensional gauge theories ..., to understand dynamical questions ..., and to extend the existence theorems from R4 to an arbitrary 4-manifold.

evidence.quote: There are many natural extensions of the Millennium problem. Among other things, one would like to prove the existence of an isolated one-particle state (an upper gap, in addition to the mass gap), to prove confinement, to prove existence of other four-dimensional gauge theories (incorporating additional fields that preserve asymptotic freedom), to understand dynamical questions (such as the possible mass gap, confinement, and chiral symmetry breaking) in these more general theories, and to extend the existence theorems from R4 to an arbitrary 4-manifold.
